meta.title: Spanish — Sounds and spelling
meta.subtitle: 27 letters, stress rules and written accents — start here, beside DELE A1
meta.desc: How Spanish is read, before or beside the first word: 27 notes, one card each — the five vowels, 16 consonant letters and pairs of letters whose sound is not the English one (b and v, c, ch, d, g, gu, h, j, ll, ñ, qu, r, rr, x, y, z), and 6 rules: where the stress falls, what the written accent is for, the words it tells apart (el and él, que and qué), and the inverted ¿ and ¡. The front shows the letters. The back gives, for each position the letter can stand in, the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet and the English sound it resembles, then up to three words of the DELE A1 deck with a speaker beside each and the letters picked out. Say the word, then press the speaker and compare. Of DELE A1's 505 words, 173 contain a letter that does not have its English value and 69 carry a written accent. THE ORDER is the vowels, the consonants in alphabetical order, then the rules. At the default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 3 days; it is meant to be studied beside DELE A1, not finished first. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: no description is written for this deck. Each context, sound and comparison is a row of the article named below, and each rule one of its sentences, with a cut marked […]. A row is carded only where a DELE A1 headword shows it, so gü has no card, and the letters that sound as an English speaker expects (f, k, l, m, n, p, s, t, w) have none. The two pronunciations of c and z are both given, Spain's first, as the article gives them. The speaker is your device's Spanish voice reading the example word, so a device without one is silent. — Sounds, comparisons and rules: Wikipedia, “Spanish orthography”, revision 1385920118 of 2026-11-15 (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words and meanings: the DELE A1 deck on this shelf (Plan curricular del Instituto Cervantes; English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Name: a word ending in a vowel, n or s
fields.Says: The default stress is on the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable on words that end in a vowel, ⟨n⟩ or ⟨s⟩ (not preceded by another consonant) […].
fields.Examples:
as in
holahello, hi, hey
graciasthank you, thanks
ahoranow, at the moment

fields.Name: a word ending in another consonant
fields.Says: The default stress is […] on the final syllable when the word ends in any consonant other than ⟨n⟩ or ⟨s⟩ or in a consonant group.
fields.Examples:
as in
hablarto speak, to talk
ustedyou (singular, formal)
la ciudadcity, town

fields.Name: the acute accent
fields.Says: Words that do not follow the default stress have an acute accent over the stressed vowel. In many cases, the accent is essential to understanding what a word means, for example hablo ‘I speak’ contrasts with habló ‘he/she/you spoke’.
fields.Examples:
as in
adiósgoodbye, farewell
tambiénalso, too, as well
el teléfonotelephone, phone

fields.Name: one-syllable words told apart by the accent
fields.Says: In eight cases, the written accent is used to distinguish stressed monosyllabic words from clitics:
fields.Pairs:
de ('of')dé ('give' or present subjunctive and imperative of 'dar')
el ('the', masculine definite article)él ('he, it' for masculine nouns)
mas ('but', archaic)más ('more')
mi ('my')mí ('me' after prepositions)
se (third person reflexive)sé ('I know' or imperative 'be')
si ('if')sí ('yes' or 'himself' after prepositions)
te (informal object case of 'you')té ('tea')
tu (informal 'your')tú (informal subject case of 'you')
fields.Examples:
as in
élhe
síyes
túyou (singular, informal)

fields.Name: question words
fields.Says: The written accent is also used in the interrogative pronouns to distinguish them from relative pronouns (which are pronounced the same but unstressed):

fields.Name: the inverted marks
fields.Says: Spanish has the unusual feature of indicating the beginning of an interrogative or exclamatory sentence or phrase with inverted variants of the question mark and exclamation mark (¿ and ¡), respectively. […] These inverted forms appear additionally at the beginning of these sentences or clauses. For example, the English phrase "How old are you?" has just the final question mark, while the Spanish equivalent, ¿Cuántos años tienes? begins with an inverted question mark.
fields.Examples:
as in
¡Hola! ¿Cómo estás?Hey! How are you doing?
¿Perdón?Pardon me?
¡Buenos días!Good morning!
